bib.title: Mirasol3B: A Multimodal Autoregressive model for time-aligned and contextual modalities

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Mirasol3B: A Multimodal Autoregressive Model for Time-Aligned and Contextual Modalities", AJ Piergiovanni, Isaac Noble, Dahun Kim, Michael S. Ryoo, Victor Gomes, Anelia Angelova (Google DeepMind / Google Research). arXiv 2311.05698v3, 3 Apr 2024 (preprint; the CVPR 2024 paper). Year 2023 (v1).

COVERAGE: All 64,844 chars read (main text, Tables 1-6, appendices A-D, references skimmed). Extraction was clean. Appendix runs to p14. No instructions embedded in the PDF text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Mirasol3B splits modelling into two autoregressive parts, one for time-aligned audio+video (chunked) and one for unaligned text, joined by cross-attention. Allocates more parameters to media.
  number: ~3B params total (2.9B without audio); "a little over half" is the audio+video model
  setup: main model
  quote: "Our model has 3B parameters; without audio it is 2.9B. A little over half of the parameters are for the audio+video autoregressive model."
  where: Sec 3.6, p5
- claim: Contrast with Flamingo, which gives only about 1% of its parameters to image/video input.
  number: ~1%
  quote: "the Flamingo model [2], subsamples the video features significantly, dedicating only about 1% of the parameters to the image and video inputs, leaving the rest for text processing."
  where: Sec 1, p2
- claim: Video is cut into T non-overlapping chunks. A Combiner compresses each chunk's video+audio features into m=32 tokens, so frame count scales without adding parameters. Default 128 frames (16 chunks x 8 frames); up to 512 (16 x 32).
  number: 128 / 512 frames; m=32
  setup: model dimension d fixed; more chunks raises memory, not parameters
  quote: "Our models work on 128 frames customarily (16 chunks, 8 frames), but can handle more for longer videos (e.g., 512=16 chunks x 32 frames). We use Combiner dimension m = 32."
  where: Sec 3.6
- claim: Memory trade-off. More chunks or frames add only marginal parameters but add memory, which is why the Combiner, and especially TTM, matters.
  quote: "Increasing the number of chunks, while not leading to parameter increases, increases memory, which underscores the importance of the Combiner and particularly the TTM."
  where: Sec 3.6
- claim: TTM Combiner (Token Turing Machine memory) saves memory and runtime versus the Transformer Combiner. Cost is constant in t. It sometimes costs accuracy.
  number: ~30% less memory, ~18% less runtime; memory 256 tokens vs ~10k history tokens
  quote: "We observe that the TTM Combiner saves memory in both training and inference, using about 30% less memory and reduces the runtime by about 18%."
  where: Sec 3.2, p4. App. C: "This reduces memory and compute use and sometimes reduces accuracy."
- claim: MSRVTT-QA (open-ended generation): Mirasol3B beats Flamingo 80B and GIT2 5B.
  number: 50.42 (Mirasol3B), 50.01 (TTM); Flamingo 47.4; GIT2 45.6; M-PLUG2 48.0
  setup: 128 frames, open-ended exact match, 3M-sample pretraining (about 12% of VTP), fine-tuned
  quote: "Mirasol3B 50.42" and "At less than 3B parameters, our model also outperforms the 5B GIT2 [51] by a large margin, and outperforms the very big Flamingo [2] of 80B parameters"
  where: Table 1 / Sec 4, p5-6
- claim: Long-video QA improves with more frames at fixed model size.
  number: ActivityNet-QA (~160 s videos): 48.25 (128 fr), 51.13 (512 fr), 49.85 (512 TTM); best prior listed UMT-L 47.9 (VideoCoca 56.1 is a classification-setting entry in gray). NExT-QA (~44 s): 68.2 (128), 72.0 (512), 73.2 (512 TTM); prior best HiTeA 63.1
  quote: "We sample up to 512 frames (e.g. 16 chunks of 32 frames each) without increasing the model size." Table 3: "Mirasol3B - 512 frames TTM 73.2" "Mirasol3B - 128 frames 68.2"
  where: Tables 2-3, p6
  note: On NExT-QA, TTM is better than the Transformer Combiner (73.2 vs 72.0); on ActivityNet it is worse (49.85 vs 51.13).
- claim: Audio+video classification is run as open-ended generation (prompt "Classify the video audio clip.", exact match on class name) and still beats SOTA.
  number: Kinetics-Sound 90.1 (A+V) vs MBT 85.0; video only 81.3. VGG-Sound 69.8 vs ONE-PEACE 68.2 (TTM 66.4). Epic-Sound A+V 78.2, TTM 79.4, video-only 72.4, audio-only 62.4 vs SSAST 53.47 / ASF 53.75
  quote: "Mirasol3B (A+V) 90.1" ; "Mirasol3B (Video) 72.4" ; "Mirasol3B (Audio) 62.4"
  where: Table 4, p6-7. Epic-Sound shows audio and video each help alone, and combined helps most.
- claim: Ablation (MSRVTT-QA, small 1.15B model, half the pretraining steps). Autoregression, Combiner and pretraining each help, and the combination helps most.
  number: baseline 41.5; +AR 43.2; +Combiner 42.1; +AR+Combiner 44.7; +pretraining 45.2; all three 47.9
  setup: 32 frames / 4 chunks
  quote: "+ AR + Comb. + PT 32/4 47.9"
  where: Table 5a
- claim: Chunking autoregressively beats one-shot processing of the full video, even at equal total feature dimension.
  number: 64 frames: 1 chunk 41.8 vs 8 chunks 45.1; 128 frames/8 chunks 45.8. Equal total dim 256 (App. B, half-epoch model): 128 frames single chunk 44.8 vs 16 chunks x 16 dim 45.5. Bidirectional variant equals autoregressive (45.1 vs 45.1)
  quote: "processing the video in chunks autoregressively in time is more advantageous than learning from the full video at once" ; "None of the single time chunk settings achieve the same performance as including a an autoregressive representation even at the same total dimensionality."
  where: Table 5c, Table 6a, App. D
- claim: Combiner design and size. Both of the authors' Combiners beat Perceiver and CLS-token variants. Output size saturates at 32.
  number: 32/4 setting: Perceiver 43.1; Transf.+CLS 43.7; Ours-Transf 44.2; Ours-TTM 44.8. Dim 8/16/32/64 = 42.53/43.36/44.20/44.22
  quote: "We chose 32 as a trade-off between sufficiently compact feature length and sufficiently expressive."
  where: Table 5b, 5d
- claim: Fine-tuning with a 10x weight on the text loss helps slightly.
  number: text loss weight 0.1 -> 44.6; 1.0 -> 45.0; 10.0 -> 45.4
  quote: "We see that increasing the weight for the text generative loss is overall beneficial."
  where: Table 6b
- claim: Input representation. Video uses sparse 3D tubes plus 2D patches through a ViT. Audio is a spectrogram whose time bands match the video's 25 fps, passed through the same ViT backbone. Each chunk's audio and video are aligned.
  number: 25 fps
  quote: "The spectrogram is created so that the time bands match the 25 frames per second used in the videos"
  where: Sec 3.1
- claim: Training recipe. Pretrained on a noisy web video-text set; most of that data has no audio, so an extra audio-only stage is needed.
  number: 3M samples (~12% of VTP); AudioSet-2M; pretrain res 224, 128 frames, lr 1e-5, batch 32; finetune res 448, lr 5e-6, wd 0.01, 10 epochs MSRVTT / 80 ActivityNet / 20 NExT; dropout 0.1, label smoothing 0.2
  quote: "Since the model is pretrained on VTP data, where most videos lack audio, we add a further audio pretraining step here. We use AudioSet-2M [14] and train the model to output the text of the class names. In this step, we freeze the weights of the model, other than the audio weights"
  where: App. D
- claim: Parameter breakdown. Text decoder ~1.3B (18 layers, d=1536); ViT-H video encoder ~630M; Combiner/causal latent/reconstruction transformers 128M each (8 layers, d=1024); audio ~100M; cross-attention 400M. Ablation model is 1.15B (ViT-L, 128M text model). Text, image backbones and cross-attention initialised from contrastively pretrained MaMMUT.
  quote: "The autoregressive text model contains about 1.3B parameters, 400M are for cross-attention weights and 400M for the vocab embeddings"
  where: App. D
- claim: Because every component is autoregressive, the model is claimed to suit streaming video (stated, not tested).
  quote: "Of note is that since all parts of the model are autoregressive, it is naturally applicable to streaming videos."
  where: Sec 3.4
- claim: Attention mask lets features inside the same chunk see each other, while keeping causality across chunks (Eq. 8). Latent loss is cosine similarity predicting the next chunk's Combiner output. Video reconstruction loss is "mostly subsumed" by it.
  where: Sec 3.3.1, 3.5

LIMITS
- Text is a global context only. ASR/subtitle text concurrent with the audio is explicitly left to future work (footnote 1, p3).
- Evaluation is exact-match open-ended generation on QA and classification benchmarks. Nothing on captioning, grounding or retrieval, and no latency or cost figures beyond the TTM memory and runtime percentages.
- Several comparisons (VideoCoca 56.1 on ActivityNet, some MSRVTT entries) use classification settings; the authors say these are advantaged. Pretraining data differ across baselines, so comparisons are not controlled.
- Ablations use a smaller 1.15B model and fewer pretraining steps. Bidirectional equals autoregressive in the ablation, so the claimed AR advantage is over non-chunked processing, not over bidirectional chunking.
- Sampling more frames on short-video benchmarks "is not productive". TTM trades accuracy for memory unevenly: it is worse on VGG-Sound (66.4 vs 69.8) and ActivityNet, better on NExT-QA and Epic-Sound.
- Overlap between chunks not used. The paper has no dedicated limitations section. The streaming claim is untested. Weights and code appear not to be released (none is mentioned).
- Dated: the 2023 baselines (Flamingo, GIT2, VideoCoca) are superseded by later native-multimodal LLMs.

BUILDS ON: Flamingo (Alayrac et al. 2022; cross-attention to the LM, Perceiver resampler); Token Turing Machines (Ryoo et al. 2022, ref [44]); TokenLearner (Ryoo et al. 2021, ref [43]); sparse 3D tubes (Piergiovanni et al. 2022, ref [39]); MaMMUT (Kuo et al. 2023, ref [23]); UAVM (Gong et al., ref [16]) for reusing the visual ViT for audio; Perceiver (Jaegle et al., ref [20]); MBT (Nagrani et al., ref [33]); Mixup (Zhang et al. 2017); SpecAugment (Park et al., ref [34]). Author names for [20], [23], [33], [34], [39], [43], [44] are inferred from the numbering and my memory of the venues, not from the extraction; check the reference list before citing.

CODE: none (paper has no code). Key equations: Combiner is causal, `x_t = Combiner(u_1, ..., u_t)` (Eq. 2). TTM: `z_t = Read(u_t, M_t); o_t = Process(z_t); M_{t+1} = Write(M_t, o_t, u_t); x_t = Output(o_t)` (Eqs 3-6). Factorisation `p(v,a) = prod_t p(v_{t+1},a_{t+1}|h_t) p(h_t|x_t) p(x_t|v_t,a_t)` (Eq. 7).

FIGURES
- Fig. 2 (p3): full architecture. Chunked audio+video model on the left, text decoder on the right, joined by cross-attention. Best single picture of the design.
- Fig. 4 (p4): Transformer Combiner vs TTM Combiner (memory read/process/write). Explains the compression and memory trade-off.
- Fig. 3 (p4): chunk-by-chunk autoregression, with Combiner outputs C_t predicting the next chunk.
- Fig. 1 (p1): conceptual split, time-aligned vs context modalities.
- Fig. 5 (p14): the four Combiner variants side by side (Transformer, TTM, CLS, Perceiver).
- Tables 2 and 3 are worth redrawing as a chart: accuracy at 128 vs 512 frames with a constant parameter count.

PROBLEMS: Table text from the extraction is flattened but readable. Table 1 has a few gray classification-setting entries that cannot be told apart in plain text. Table 2 lists VideoCoca at 56.1 in the same list as the other baselines. Footnote text has a typo, "0.75%" for the masking ratio, which is probably a ratio of 0.75 (the paper's own wording: "random masking to the Combiner output features at a ratio of 0.75%"). No embedded instructions found.
